title: Incremental Answer Staging — Lab Journal
body:
Context and quick pitch:

This is a personal lab / scratchpad exploring a UX + runtime pattern I keep bumping into: "incremental answer staging" — the system surfaces a compact, high-confidence snippet quickly, followed by progressively richer expansions (detail sections, citations, optional deep-dive transforms). Goal: reduce perceived latency and token costs for applications that only sometimes need full-fidelity output.

Motivation / observed problems:
- Users often accept a short, correct answer and only occasionally ask for more. But our single-shot full-generation emits a large token payload every time, increasing cost and latency.
- In chat scenarios, the first response is perceived as slow even when subsequent tokens stream; sometimes a short snippet would be enough.
- Current fallback/fidelity features (economy modes, model routing) are coarse-grained and require product-level plumbing (two separate requests, client orchestration).

Core idea (very rough):
1) Fast-stage (T0): return a compact, high-precision snippet/summary (1–3 sentences) from a low-latency/low-cost model variant or cached prefix. This must be produced within a tight SLO (e.g., 200–350ms p95).
2) Expand-stage (T1+): if the user requests more detail, or heuristics indicate they will, fetch an expanded payload (paragraphs, code, citations) possibly from a higher-fidelity model or by re-running the prompt with extended context.
3) Optional background fill: asynchronously compute a full expanded result and attach it to logs/analytics or pre-warm user's session cache so future requests can be faster.

Why this is different from existing fallbacks:
- It treats the initial snippet as a first-class product surface (not just a truncated stream).
- It exposes an explicit API contract: clients can render the snippet immediately and decide whether to request expansions.
- It supports server-side heuristics to auto-upgrade expansions when signals predict high value (e.g., user dwell, complex query features).

User stories (proto):
- As a consumer-facing chat UI, I want to show an immediate one-line answer while the full article is loading so the user feels the system is responsive.
- As a mobile client, I want to avoid pulling a large token payload unless the user taps "More" to save bandwidth.
- As a platform engineer, I want this to run with a single API call (or one coordinated call from the platform) so app authors don't have to implement complicated orchestration.

API sketch (brainstorm):
- POST /responses.incremental { prompt, stage_config: { initial_model: "redwood-lite-1", initial_max_tokens: 48, expansion_model: "redwood-precise-2", expansion_max_tokens: 512, expansion_mode: "on_demand|auto|background" }, client_hint: {mobile:true} }
- Response: { request_id, initial_output: { text, confidence_score?, tokens }, expansion_handle: { id: "exp-...", status: "pending|ready|skipped" }, suggested_client_actions: ["tap_more", "open_details"] }
- GET /responses.expansions/{id} to fetch expanded payload when ready or after user action.

Runtime considerations:
- We can implement as two internal executions: a very cheap first-pass generation using quantized model / cached completions, and a second execution when needed. Need wiring for request correlation + consistent provenance (so expansions include the same system prompt + deterministic seed if possible).
- KV/prefix caching: use per-session prefix caches to synthesize initial_output for frequent prompts (FAQ-like).
- Batching: initial stage must prioritize low-latency routing; expansion stage can be batched for throughput.
- Cost accounting: charge initial tokens + additional tokens only when expansion is served (or prorate for background precompute). Need clear product-level metering semantics.

Metrics to track in an experiment:
- p50/p95 latency of initial_output vs full_response baseline
- fraction of sessions where expansion is requested (conversion rate)
- tokens consumed per session and cost delta vs baseline
- user engagement metrics: retention of users who got initial snippet first vs baseline
- correctness/regression signal: compare initial_output accuracy vs full_response accuracy on eval sets

Risks / open questions:
- UX confusion: splitting content could feel fragmented if transitions are janky.
- Consistency: expansions must not contradict initial snippet. If they do, user trust suffers.
- Edge cases: code snippets or structured outputs that cannot be meaningfully truncated into a snippet.
- Billing complexity for customers and for self-serve console—need to decide how initial + expansion pricing is surfaced.

Experiment variants to try quickly (MVPs):
A) Client-driven two-call flow: simple prototype where UI explicitly calls initial then on-demand expansion. Fast to test but pushes complexity to app teams.
B) Server-coordinated optimistic background: server triggers a background expansion after initial_output and stores it; client can poll. Tests fewer app changes but uses extra compute.
C) Heuristic auto-upgrade: server uses signals (query length, category, user history) to auto-run expansion for queries likely to need detail.

Prototype plan (2–3 sprints rough):
- Sprint 1: minimal API + client demo (web widget) using two-call flow (A). Instrument metrics.
- Sprint 2: add server-side background precompute (B) and small heuristic model to auto-upgrade for long queries. Compare cost.
- Sprint 3: polish API ergonomics, add console visualization for expansion conversion, introduce conservative billing model for expansion tokens.

Immediate next steps (today / this week):
- Sync with Ravi (infra) on feasibility of low-latency micro-model routing and session prefix caching.
- Sketch a toy widget that calls initial then expansion on user click (Talia volunteered a quick front-end mock).
- Draft a tiny evaluation prompt-set (50 queries) with target gold expansions to measure accuracy of initial snippets.

Notes / random thoughts:
- Could borrow "card" UX pattern: initial_output is a card summary with inline CTA (More, Cite, Expand to code).
- Consider a generic "stages" primitive in Redwood API so other patterns (preview -> full, summary -> expanded sections) can reuse same semantics.
- For private/VPC customers with strict billing, provide a toggle to disable background precompute.

Stuff to surface later in a PRD: billing behavior, observability hooks (per-stage token breakdown), sample code for clients (web/mobile), recommended heuristics for auto-upgrade, privacy/compliance implications for background work.

Open questions I want to answer in the prototype:
- How often is initial snippet "enough"? (target: >60% for FAQs/simple Q&A)
- Does perceived latency drop more with a tiny snippet vs streaming first 1s of tokens?
- Can we ensure expansions are deterministic enough to avoid contradictions?

Parking lot ideas (not for MVP):
- "Peek and replace": edit-in-place where initial snippet is editable by user and used as partial prompt for expansion.
- Server-side diffing: show only the delta between snippet and expansion to reduce client rendering size.
- Prefetch expansions for frequent repeat visitors automatically on low-cost windows.

Personal takeaways: this feels like a pragmatic lever to improve perceived latency + reduce token costs without forcing app teams into complex model switching. Need to be ruthless about UX polishes (animations, strong CTA) so this doesn't feel like a half-broken experience.

---
Outgoing: will turn the two-call widget into a morning demo for platform sync on Tuesday. If anyone wants to scribble on the API sketch or volunteer to run the 50-query eval, ping me in slack (michelle.g).
